facts.claim: The Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey (PMMS) 30-year fixed mortgage rate average was 6.66% for the week ending 2026-07-30.
facts.source: Freddie Mac PMMS, via FRED (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis), series MORTGAGE30US
facts.note: Used as the real current interest rate assumption for both worked examples below. This is a real, dated, weekly-updated rate, not a rounded or invented figure - script must state it is a real recent average, not a rate any individual borrower is guaranteed.

facts.claim: On a new $400,000, 30-year mortgage at 6.66%, paying an extra $300/month starting immediately pays the loan off in 22 years 5 months (7 years 7 months earlier) and saves $155,461 in total interest (30% less interest: $525,383 -> $369,922). Monthly payment rises from $2,570.51 to $2,870.51.
facts.source: Calculator.net Mortgage Payoff Calculator (standard amortization math)
facts.status: [VERIFIED - computed live via the calculator's own form, 2026-08-04]
facts.computed_check: Original total interest $525,382.78 on $400k/30yr/6.66% matches standard amortization formula for those inputs (monthly payment $2,570.51 x 360 - 400,000 = $525,383.60, matches within rounding).

facts.claim: Same $400,000/30-year/6.66% loan: paying one extra full payment a year ($2,571, once annually - the classic '13th payment' strategy) instead of $300/month pays the loan off in 24 years 3 months (5 years 9 months earlier) and saves $117,987 in interest (22% less interest).
facts.status: [VERIFIED - computed live via the calculator's own form, 2026-08-04]
facts.note: Two different real strategies on the identical loan, used to show the mechanism scales with however much extra principal a viewer can actually pay, not just one magic number.

facts.claim: On the $400,000/30-year/6.66% loan, the month-1 payment of $2,570.51 splits to approximately $2,220.00 interest (400,000 x 0.0666/12) and approximately $350.51 principal - about 86% interest in the first month.
facts.status: illustrative:true - derived with the standard amortization formula (interest = prior balance x monthly rate) from the already-verified loan terms, not a new external source

facts.claim: A smaller $250,000, 30-year loan at the same 6.66% rate, with an extra $200/month starting immediately, pays off in 22 years 1 month (7 years 11 months earlier) and saves $101,429 in interest (31% less: $328,364 -> $226,935).
facts.status: [VERIFIED - computed live via the calculator's own form, 2026-08-04]
facts.note: Used to show the mechanism scales down to a smaller, more relatable loan size, not just the $400k headline example.

facts.claim: Same $400,000/30-year/6.66% loan, paid biweekly instead of monthly ($1,285.25 every two weeks, which is half the monthly payment but produces 26 payments a year instead of 24 half-payments, i.e. one extra full payment a year): payoff in 24 years 2 months (5 years 10 months earlier), saving $120,479 in interest (23% less).
facts.status: [VERIFIED - computed live via the calculator's own form, 2026-08-04]
facts.note: Nearly identical result to payoff-one-extra-payment-per-year (24yr3mo / $117,987) - used to make the point that biweekly payment plans are not a separate trick, they are the same one-extra-payment-a-year mechanism, automated by the payment schedule.

dropped_or_softened: Did not claim 6.66% as a rate any specific viewer will get - real mortgage rates vary by credit score, loan type, and lender; framed as 'a real, recent national average', not a personal quote.

Did not claim extra payments are always the right move - the honest-limits beat weighs this against investing the same money at the market's historical average (10.87%/yr, per money-archive-compound-interest's own sourced S&P 500 figure) and against having an adequate emergency fund first, per honesty_guard.
